name: Apple IIc
summary: A compact, all-in-one Apple II designed for education and the home, and the machine many visitors remember from their own classroom.
significance: The Apple IIc made serious computing power approachable for students, educators, and small businesses. Its built-in disk drive, integrated design, and full backward compatibility with the enormous Apple II software library helped define a generation of learning, creativity, and early desktop publishing.

name: Apple IIe
summary: The 'Enhanced' successor to the original Apple II, and the longest-lived model in the II family — sold for over a decade in schools nationwide.
significance: Its expansion slots and durability made the IIe a mainstay of American classrooms well into the 1990s, long after flashier machines had come and gone.

name: Apple Lisa
summary: One of the first commercial computers to popularize a graphical user interface and mouse — a commercial disappointment that reshaped the industry anyway.
significance: At $9,995 the Lisa was too expensive to succeed commercially, but its windows-icons-mouse interface previewed the direction the entire industry would follow.

specs.Storage: Twin 5.25" 'Twiggy' drives / ProFile 5 MB hard disk

name: IBM 5150 Personal Computer
summary: The machine that gave the 'PC' its name — IBM's entry into personal computing set the open-architecture standard the industry still follows.
significance: By publishing the 5150's technical specifications, IBM enabled a vast ecosystem of compatible hardware and software — the 'IBM-compatible PC' — that continues to shape computing today.

name: IBM 1401 Data Processing System
summary: One of the most widely used computers of the early 1960s, the 1401 brought affordable data processing to thousands of businesses.
significance: Its transistorized design and low relative cost made electronic data processing practical for ordinary businesses for the first time, not just governments and giant corporations.

name: DEC PDP-8/e (“SID”)
summary: A workhorse 12-bit minicomputer nicknamed “SID” by RICM volunteers, restored and maintained in running condition.
significance: The PDP-8 family made interactive computing affordable outside of giant institutional data centers, seeding the minicomputer industry that DEC would come to dominate.

specs.Notes: Restored to running condition by RICM volunteers

name: DEC PDP-9
summary: An 18-bit successor to the PDP-7, currently undergoing an ongoing volunteer restoration effort documented in RICM's restoration log.
significance: Represents DEC's continued push toward interactive, real-time computing for laboratories and research institutions.

name: Eagle Business Computer
summary: An early CP/M-based business computer from a short-lived but notable competitor in the pre-IBM-PC office-computing market.
significance: Illustrates the crowded, fast-moving small-systems market that existed just before the IBM PC standardized the industry.

name: DIGI-COMP I
summary: A mechanical, plastic digital computer sold as an educational toy — no electricity required. Visitors flip its logic gates by hand.
significance: One of the first devices to teach the general public — including children — the fundamentals of binary logic and digital computation, entirely through mechanical linkages.

specs.Notes: Marketed directly to schools and hobbyists

name: Commodore 64
summary: The best-selling single computer model of all time, prized for its sound and graphics chips as much as its low price.
significance: With over 12 million units sold, the C64 introduced a generation to home computing, programming, and gaming simultaneously.

name: TRS-80 Model I
summary: Sold through thousands of ordinary RadioShack storefronts, the TRS-80 was many first-time buyers' introduction to owning a computer.
significance: Alongside the Apple II and Commodore PET, the TRS-80 formed the '1977 Trinity' that launched the mass-market home computer industry.

name: Atari 2600
summary: The cartridge-based console that made video games a living-room fixture across America.
significance: Its interchangeable-cartridge design created the model the entire games industry still follows.

name: TI-99/4A
summary: A 16-bit home computer years ahead of most 8-bit competitors on paper, sold at a loss in a bruising price war with Commodore.
significance: Its early 16-bit processor and speech-synthesis add-on made it a technically ambitious entrant in the early home-computer wars.

name: HP-35 Calculator
summary: The first handheld scientific calculator, retiring the slide rule in engineering programs almost overnight.
significance: Its introduction is widely credited with ending the slide rule's century-long reign as the engineer's essential tool.

name: Xerox Alto
summary: Never sold commercially, the Alto pioneered the graphical user interface, mouse, and Ethernet networking that would define computing for decades.
significance: Nearly every desktop-computing convention in use today — windows, icons, a mouse pointer, WYSIWYG editing — traces to the Alto.

name: Sinclair ZX81
summary: An ultra-low-cost British computer sold as a kit or assembled, credited with introducing an enormous number of UK households to computing.
significance: Its touch-membrane keyboard and rock-bottom price made it one of the cheapest paths into home computing anywhere in the world.

name: Osborne 1
summary: Widely considered the first commercially successful portable computer — 'luggable' rather than lightweight, at nearly 24 pounds.
significance: It bundled a full software suite with the hardware, an early example of value pricing that reshaped how computers were sold.
